utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, did the owner of the house live in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether he came from time to time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether he came, whether he spent some time in the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he did not stay in the house. Whether occasionally he came to the house, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you finally leave that house? When did you move out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st or the 22nd of July, 1998. I cannot recall the exact day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you used this house for about two years after the war had been completed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go straight to the United States after you left this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first went to Belgrade, and from Belgrade to the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon leaving the house, did you hand the house over to the Ministry for Displaced Persons or to the owner of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I handed it over to the person who was living in the other half of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the owner of the house had submitted the request for the house to be returned to him by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the property that you had found in the house, such as furniture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the furniture was taken over by the person who occupied the other half of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with the rest of the things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sold the refrigerator and the freezer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sold the things that did not belong to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this, too, had been brought over from another house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you decide to go to the United States?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife's family, all of them, are there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of your past, of the involvement in the events in Zvornik during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, if I was aware of it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that it was possible for you to -- for your past to be disclosed once you submitted your application to go to the United States?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn the question around. Did you think that by going to the United States you were not going to be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I simply couldn't imagine that it would come to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that in 1998 you did not feel guilty, you personally, privately, that you did not have such feelings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what passport, issued by which state, did you go to the United States?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they let you in without a travel document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all arranged for through the immigration agency of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's why you didn't need a travel document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then. Now, you were first contacted by the investigators in the month of August 2002, I mean the investigators of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They wanted an interview with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what the subject of the conversation would be before you proceeded with this interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that you were a suspect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And despite the caution, you, as you acknowledged, did not tell the truth on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't tell the truth because you wanted to play down your responsibility for the events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of the direct involvement and my direct link with the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying that at the time you decided to go to the United States you did not think of that possibility, you did not have that possibility in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December, 2003, you gave another statement to the investigators. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, you are aware of the fact that you're a suspect. Once again, they caution you of your rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once again you decide not to tell the truth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I understand that it is difficult for you to answer these questions, but once again, is the reason for which you're not telling the truth again your involvement in the events and your attempts to play down the responsibility that you had in the events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to present the last document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour. The question is worded improperly, and it may be a function of translation. But the reason you are not telling the truth, that is a suggestion that he is not telling the truth today, so that is improper. It may just be a translation issue. I don't think that Mr. Stojanovic means to be saying -- saying that, but that's what the English says, that "you're not telling the truth."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's concerning about the statement that the witness made on the 3rd of December, 2003. Am I right? Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record, yes, I was referring to the statement given on the 3rd of December, 2003. And the answer is correctly reflected in the transcript, to avoid any misunderstanding. And thank you for this intervention because I have a language problem here. I should like to produce one more exhibit that we have. Your Honour, it would be perhaps wise to move into private session for this purpose, in light of the contents of the document that we are going to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And before the re-direct, Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask you a question concerning the documents. The map of the location inside the security officer's office of the Zvornik Brigade, what's the number of that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, D63/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the document you just used? Were there any numbers attached to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. For the purposes of identification, we used number 67/3, and we would like to tender this document into evidence. And we know that the document is probably going to be used by the other party. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-direct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you or Mr. Popovic ever come up with any kind of a rough estimate of the number of victims in the primary graves of Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, and Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you relate to us what those estimates were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Popovic told me -- I know that at the Orahovac gym, there were between 5 and 600 detained Muslims from Srebrenica. He also told me that there were about the same number of Muslims at Petkovci and Rocevic, whereas in Branjevo there were twice as many. Some were between 15 and 1800.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think the information was vital to the Prosecution and, you know, for the purposes of this trial. However, I just wish to note that this question was beyond the scope of cross-examination. I know it's a technical issue, but I would appreciate if there are going to be questions that are beyond the scope on rebuttal, that at least permission be sought before asking such questions. But I do appreciate Mr. McCloskey's need to get that information out. I just think that it was beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think during the cross-examination, the number murdered in Orahovac was mentioned several times. And as for the other places, I do not have that recollection. But since this question is raised, I will give the opportunity for the Defence, if they need, to cross this issue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not -- Mr. President, I'm not requesting any additional -- I thought it was -- this might have been pertinent information to be sought on direct examination. And I think because it was, I did not object to it at this point in time. I'm merely pointing a technicality. In the past when I have been asked whether I wanted to cross-examination or re-cross, I indicated it was going to be beyond the scope, at which point I was denied that opportunity. So that was merely a technicality, although, as I said, I understand Mr. McCloskey's need to have that information. And I concur that it is important information to have in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. As they were going over the real detail of the reburial process, it dawned on me that there was other details related to that process that should be asked and that I had not asked. So I think it's, like a lot of things, a combination of yes, it was dealt with on direct, and yes, Mr. Karnavas is right, in a perfect world I would have remembered everything. But I think it is perfectly acceptable re-direct for the reasons that you have stated and those that I have stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that's purely a legal issue. There's no dispute concerning with this practical manner, and I would like to thank Mr. Karnavas for reminding us of this point. Any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge Vassylenko. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My first question is: How many Muslim prisoners would there be on each bus that arrived at Orahovac school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many of them were in each of the buses, perhaps 30 to 50. I don't know exactly because they arrived at night and I didn't send them off. I didn't escort them. Only I saw them when there were at there at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Were the buses re-used several times or did they only go once each to the collection site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this operation, the organisation of the transportation and the transportation site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You have testified that two groups of reinforcements arrived, one from Lazarevic and one from Ristic. Before this group arrived, how many soldiers provided security at the Orahovac school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, six, or seven. I don't know the exact number. That's an approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And my last question: Do you have specific evidence indicating direct and active involvement of Colonel Blagojevic in the murder operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any evidence of the involvement of Blagojevic in the murder operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Hvala, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, three documents under seal. 699 is the indictment from the U.S., 700 is the record of judgement of conviction of that indictment, and 701 is the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please repeat the numbers, because I got several copies with different numbers, so I'm a little bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We had a little glitch there, but the indictment is 699, the judgement is 700, and the pseudonym sheet is 701.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Something is wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We had a problem and then we -- Janet submitted another sheet. She apparently made a mistake, which I'm sure won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Technically speaking, no. However, I don't see the need why we need the indictment or the judgement in. I think we have direct testimony from the witness that he was indicted, that he was sentenced -- well, in effect, he was turned over to the custody of immigration. So I don't see the purpose of adding more paperwork to the paperwork. But technically speaking, I don't object to it. I just don't think it's necessary. As far as 701, obviously, there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, would you please tell us the reason we see -- it seems to us that there's no need to admit those two documents into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are very serious documents and are reflected in the testimony, of course. And my -- and just for the reason about complete openness, so the Court was aware of this material, I offered it in. If the Court doesn't feel it necessary, I would withdraw it. But I do believe it's important in relation to the entire situation here, so you have a complete record of it. But again, it's -- I'm -- I'm fine either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any objections to these three documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We don't have any objections to these documents. We also feel that there is no need for the judgement to be admitted, because it is not the subject of any debate or dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we believe that the document 701 is admitted into the evidence under seal. And document P699 and P700 are not admitted into evidence. And, Mr. Karnavas, I think you told us that you have no evidence to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We just want to have it confirmed. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I tender into evidence Exhibit D63/3, that is a diagram of the premises of the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade; then I also wish to tender into evidence document marked as D67/3, that is the memo from the military public prosecutor dated 26th of March, 1996; and we also wish to have admitted into evidence - although I am aware of the attitude that the Trial Chamber has taken in this regard - D68/3, that is a segment of the statement of Tanacko Tanic, dated 24th of June, 2002, that was given to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. Okay, so that is not the statement, because I know that the Trial Chamber has ruled that it doesn't want to have any statements admitted, but just this segment of the statement. All the other evidence that we used in our examination are in fact already part of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no objection to the sketch. However, portions of an interview of a witness that has not testified I would object to. If there is some value to portions, it should be -- the whole thing should come in, but that opens up another set of issues. And it's not like the statements that we had of Mr. Deronjic, who was here and who testified. I don't know if we'll see this man or not, Mr. Tanic, and I - without some further clarification of the relevancy of a portion - I would object -- I'm sorry. And the order regarding the number D67/3, which was the military prosecutor document, I have no problem with. It was D68/3, the Tanic statement that my comments should have been directed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the document D63/3, the sketch, as well as the document D67/3 are admitted into the evidence. The document D68/3 is not admitted into the evidence because we believe that all the relevant parts have been brought up during the cross-examination. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for your coming to The Hague to give your testimony. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. I wish you a pleasant journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ms. Davis will be handling the next witness, and if I could be excused for the rest of the evening, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good evening, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Davis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good evening, Witness. Would you please state your name for the record and spell it.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Novak Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind spelling it.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: N-o-v-a-k.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last name, sir.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: K-o-v-a-c-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand that you're a lawyer by profession?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I am currently the district public prosecutor of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long have you served in that position?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Since the 1st of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a few questions about your background. I understand you received your law degree in 1976 from the University of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you thereafter served for a number of years as a basic public prosecutor and a judge in Rogatica municipality?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you begin service within the military court system of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I became a military public prosecutor in April, year 2000, in the VRS. Before that, I worked in the military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the VRS, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court briefly what position you held, beginning in May 1992, and your subsequent positions within the VRS military court system.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, this was still -- in fact, when the war broke out, I was the municipal public prosecutor in Rogatica, that was at the very beginning of the war. I was never relieved of my duty there, but when the call-up was effected, I reported to Han Pijesak. And in those days, the military judicial system of the Republika Srpska was beginning to be formed, and I was appointed a judge of the Srpsko Sarajevo military court. That was sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you serve as a judge in the military court in Srpsko Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go subsequent to that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was appointed a judge of the VRS supreme military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1993. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the supreme military court located at that time, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in that position as a judge of the supreme military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Up until April 2000. Until I was appointed to the position of the prosecutor of the VRS, the VRS military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the headquarters of the supreme military court, did it remain in Han Pijesak throughout the entire period that you served as a judge there?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not. It was moved to Zvornik. I believe it was in 1994. And it remained there until it was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention that in April 2000 you were appointed as the military prosecutor for the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your -- well, I'll leave that for a moment. How long did you serve in that position?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not for long, because sometime in May - I think it was the 25th of May, but that's not important - the military judiciary was dissolved. It no longer existed. But up until September that year, we had to effect the handover of all our cases to the normal civilian courts, according to their territorial jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I have understood the chronology, in July 1995 you held the position of judge of the supreme military court, which was then located in Zvornik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what your responsibilities were as a judge on the supreme military court.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked cases which mostly dealt with the appeals to judgements and various decisions, because the court of the first instance would deal with all those cases in the first instance. And then the supreme court would deal with all the appeals. That is mostly what I did, and so did my colleagues, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any investigative responsibilities as a judge at the supreme military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, because investigations were carried out by the basic courts, the first instance courts. We dealt with appeals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Focusing on the period 1995 for a moment, can you tell us how many basic military courts were there in the Republika Srpska, the military court system.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In 1995 the basic courts within the military judicial system were located in Bijeljina, Banja Luka, Bileca, and now I don't remember exactly whether that -- it was that year or perhaps a while later. The basic military court of Srpsko Sarajevo was dissolved. I don't know, as I said, if it was in that period of time, but more or less it was at that time period. And all the cases from the basic military court of Srpsko Sarajevo were transferred to Bijeljina and Bileca, depending on the place where the criminal offenses had been committed. So again we have this territorial jurisdiction principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken a couple of times about the territorial jurisdiction issue. Can you tell us what determined the parameters of these districts you've just described.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the law on criminal procedure and law on courts. In other words, the location where a crime was committed dictated the jurisdiction of the court. The court that had jurisdiction over that area -- district municipality adjudicated in those cases. As far as military courts were concerned, their jurisdiction coincided with the areas of responsibility of the corps. For instance, at the beginning the Sarajevo court covered the area of responsibility of Sarajevo-Romanija corps. Whereas the one in Banja Luka, the Krajina corps; the one in Bileca the Hercegovina corps; and the one in Bijeljina covered the East Bosnia corps. Later on the Drina Corps was established, and for a time until it was dissolved was covered by the military court in Srpsko Sarajevo. So the -- this did not coincide. As far as the territorial jurisdiction of the two sets of court, the civilian and the military courts, did not coincide. Because military courts dealt with the cases from their respective corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the Drina Corps was under the jurisdiction of the Srpsko Sarajevo court, until that district, that Srpsko Sarajevo court district was dissolved. Can you tell us in July 1995 which military court district had jurisdiction over the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm trying to explain. I cannot exactly remember at this point, but it should be found somewhere in the documents, I mean, the date when the basic military court of Srpsko Sarajevo was dissolved. I don't know whether this was before or after July 1995. I cannot remember the exact date. So before it was dissolved, it was the basic military court of Srpsko Sarajevo that had territorial jurisdiction over the Drina Corps. But if this was after the dissolution of the Sarajevo -- Srpsko Sarajevo court, then the Drina Corps would be under the jurisdiction of the Bijeljina basic military court. Part of the cases, because apart from the territories you're interested in, Srebrenica and Bratunac, this also included Vlasenica and Milici. When the Drina Corps was dissolved, then Vlasenica and Milici, that is the cases from the area relating to the area of Vlasenica and Milici were not transferred to Bijeljina, but to Srpsko Sarajevo court. Now, this only concerns Vlasenica and Milici. Because the area is now part of the Srpsko or was now part of the Srpsko Sarajevo district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So crimes committed by VRS personnel in and around Srebrenica, Vlasenica, Zvornik in July 1995 would either have been under the jurisdiction of the Bijeljina district if the Srpsko Sarajevo court had already been dissolved, or if that court may not have been dissolved, they may have been under the jurisdiction of the Srpsko Sarajevo district at that time. Is that a correct summary of what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was not able to translate everything and is kindly asking you to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Davis, you go too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to crimes committed, any crimes that may have been committed by VRS personnel in July 1995 in and around Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, I believe what you've told us is that the military court district that would have had jurisdiction would either have been the Bijeljina district or the Srpsko Sarajevo district, unless that district had been dissolved prior to 1995, July 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the Srpsko Sarajevo district was dissolved prior to July 1995, then the Bijeljina district would have had jurisdiction over those cases?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 -- not the district court in Bijeljina, but the military court in Bijeljina. We're still talking about military courts at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Of course.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The cases from Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik would be dealt with by the military court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the records for many cases in the Srpsko Sarajevo court as you've said were transferred to the Bijeljina district after that first court was dissolved. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I explained a moment ago, those cases were transferred from the area covered by the Bijeljina district. I'm referring to Zvornik, Srebrenica, and Bratunac. The cases relating to that area went to Bijeljina. And the ones that were completed, the pending ones, all that went to the district military prosecutor in Bijeljina. The same was done with respect of the cases concerning Vlasenica and Milici, who were transferred to the court in Srpsko Sarajevo district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You have mentioned that the supreme military court -- sorry. You've mentioned that the supreme military court on which you served as a judge was located in Zvornik. Where were your offices precisely?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Our offices were in the centre of the Zvornik town, in the building of the former IZVOR company, not far from the town hall, the police. This is where the court had its seat, not only the court but also the prosecutor's office and the military court as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the military prosecutor's offices were in the same building as your building?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much contact, if any, did you have as a judge with the military prosecutors and the military legal staff in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had contact with them throughout that time, in 1995, and later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also told us that you later served yourself as a military prosecutor for a brief period in the year 2000. Can you tell us what your responsibilities were as the, as I understand it, the chief military prosecutor for the VRS.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the prosecutor of the VRS for a brief period of time, as I told you. My responsibilities included providing opinion concerning cases that reached us as well as the appeals. And in light of the system of subordination, we had control over them -- I mean, we were above them. I'm talking about the prosecutors. And we were able to issue certain instructions to them and to have consultations regarding the cases that they wanted to hear our opinion of. This was sometimes submitted in writing or it was done orally. I'm referring to the military prosecutor of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony, are you referring to the basic military prosecutors and some sort of supervisory role of those basic military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to the basic military prosecutors. At the time there were three, Bijeljina, Banja Luka, and Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of -- in your role as superior or supervisor or the basic military prosecutors, what sort of contact did you have with them, whether oral or written?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly these were oral contacts, but there were written contacts as well. As I indicated, I spent only one month in this capacity. The office was very soon dissolved, and we were instructed to finish, or rather, prepare the cases in order to hand them over.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to address some documents which the first document may take more than the remaining time, so I'm happy to begin and pick up tomorrow, or we can break. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, Witness, while you are in The Hague, you have to remember that you are still under oath. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. You must understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we'll resume tomorrow morning 9.00 in the same courtroom. The hearing for today is adjourned.
